# The question {.unnumbered}

## What this note assumes

This is the most advanced supporting note, but it is written to explain the
language rather than prove a consistency theorem. Read

- [Lebesgue measure, null sets, and almost surely](lebesgue-measure-integration-and-densities.qmd);
- [what $\Pi(df\mid X)$ means](../Bayesian/bayes-measure-d-concept.qmd);
- [KL divergence](../Other/km-divergence.qmd)

first. No prior course in topology or empirical-process theory is assumed.

Suppose the observations really are iid from a fixed distribution $P_0$ with
density $f_0$. The asymptotic question is whether, as $n$ grows, the posterior
puts most of its mass near $f_0$.

The word **near** needs a topology, metric, or divergence. Posterior consistency
is therefore inseparable from how neighborhoods of distributions are defined.

These terms play related but different roles:

- a **metric** is a numerical distance satisfying symmetry and the triangle
  inequality;
- a **divergence** is a numerical discrepancy that may lack those properties,
  as KL does;
- a **topology** specifies which sets count as neighborhoods and therefore what
  convergence means, even when no particular numerical distance is emphasized.

For this note, you can think of a neighborhood as a declared meaning of “close
to $f_0$.”

# Two probability laws must be distinguished {#consistency-two-laws}

## The Bayesian model

The Bayesian hierarchy is

$$
f\sim\Pi,
\qquad
X_i\mid f\overset{\mathrm{iid}}\sim f.
$$

Integrating out $f$ gives the prior-predictive joint law

$$
m_n(x_{1:n})
=\int\prod_{i=1}^nf(x_i)\Pi(df).
$$

## The sampling law used to study repeated data

For frequentist evaluation of the Bayesian learning rule, fix a true density
$f_0$ and assume

$$
X_1,X_2,\ldots\overset{\mathrm{iid}}\sim f_0.
$$

The probability law of the infinite data sequence is denoted

$$
P_0^\infty=\bigotimes_{i=1}^{\infty}P_0.
$$

The symbol $\bigotimes$ denotes a **product probability measure**, not ordinary
multiplication. It is the one probability law governing the whole infinite
sequence $(X_1,X_2,\ldots)$ when every coordinate has distribution $P_0$ and
the coordinates are independent. For a finite rectangular event,

$$
P_0^\infty(X_1\in A_1,\ldots,X_n\in A_n)
=\prod_{i=1}^nP_0(A_i).
$$

The infinite notation lets one make a single “almost sure as $n\to\infty$”
statement about the entire sequence.

The prior-predictive law and $P_0^\infty$ serve different purposes. We need not
pretend that Nature sampled $f_0$ from our subjective prior in order to ask
whether the resulting posterior learns under repeated data from $f_0$.

# General consistency statement {#consistency-statement}

Let $d$ be a distance or let $U_\varepsilon(f_0)$ be a chosen neighborhood.
Posterior consistency at $f_0$ means that for every $\varepsilon>0$,

$$
\boxed{
\Pi\{f:d(f,f_0)>\varepsilon\mid X_{1:n}\}
\longrightarrow0
}
\quad P_0^\infty\text{-almost surely}.
\tag{1}
$$

Equivalently,

$$
\Pi\{f:d(f,f_0)<\varepsilon\mid X_{1:n}\}
\longrightarrow1.
$$

“$P_0^\infty$-almost surely” means that the convergence may fail for a set of
infinite data sequences whose probability under repeated sampling from $P_0$
is zero.

This is the probability version of “almost everywhere.” It does not mean that
$f_0$ was randomly sampled from the prior. The randomness in (1) comes from
the repeated data sequence.

# Common ways to define nearness

Assume $f$ and $g$ are densities relative to a common measure $\nu$.

## L1 distance

$$
d_1(f,g)=\int|f-g|\,d\nu.
$$

For probability densities, $0\leq d_1(f,g)\leq2$.

## Total-variation distance

$$
d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)
=\sup_A|P(A)-Q(A)|
=\frac12\int|f-g|\,d\nu.
$$

Total variation controls the largest probability discrepancy over all
measurable events.

The supremum $\sup_A$ means the largest possible value as $A$ ranges over all
measurable events. Thus total variation asks for the event on which $P$ and
$Q$ disagree most strongly.

## Hellinger distance

One common convention is

$$
h^2(f,g)
=\frac12\int\{\sqrt{f}-\sqrt{g}\}^2d\nu.
\tag{2}
$$

Other authors omit the factor $1/2$. Always check the convention. Hellinger
distance is popular in nonparametric asymptotics because it is bounded and
interacts well with likelihood ratios and tests.

## KL divergence

$$
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(f_0\|f)
=\int f_0\log\frac{f_0}{f}\,d\nu.
$$

KL is not a metric, but KL neighborhoods are central support conditions.

## Weak neighborhoods {#weak-neighborhoods}

A sequence $P_n$ converges weakly to $P$ if

$$
\int\varphi\,dP_n\to\int\varphi\,dP
$$

for every bounded continuous $\varphi$. Weak convergence is weaker than total
variation or Hellinger convergence. It controls smooth bounded summaries, not
every event probability or density feature.

“Bounded” means $|\varphi(x)|$ stays below some finite constant; “continuous”
has its ordinary calculus meaning. Weak convergence therefore compares
averages of a broad class of stable summaries. For example,
$N(a,\sigma_n^2)$ distributions with $\sigma_n^2\to0$ converge weakly to a
Dirac point mass at $a$, even though a continuous distribution and a point
mass are very different in total variation.

# Relationships worth remembering

Under common domination and the convention in (2), inequalities such as

$$
h^2(P,Q)\leq d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)
$$

and Pinsker's inequality

$$
d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)
\leq\sqrt{\frac12D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)}
$$

show that small KL implies small total variation, which implies small
Hellinger distance. Converses do not hold without additional conditions.

The exact constants depend on the Hellinger convention.

The inequalities are optional on a first reading. Their conceptual message is
that the word “consistent” is incomplete unless the mode of closeness is
specified; some modes demand substantially more than others.

# Prior support {#prior-support}

No posterior can learn a region that the prior rules out. A basic necessary
idea is therefore that the prior put positive mass in every relevant
neighborhood of $f_0$.

## Topological support

For a chosen metric $d$, $f_0$ lies in the support of $\Pi$ if

$$
\Pi\{f:d(f,f_0)<\varepsilon\}>0
\quad\text{for every }\varepsilon>0.
$$

This does not require $\Pi(\{f_0\})>0$, which is usually zero for a continuous
or infinite-dimensional prior. It requires positive prior probability in
every nonzero-radius neighborhood around $f_0$.

## KL support {#consistency-kl-support}

$f_0$ lies in the KL support of $\Pi$ if

$$
\Pi\left\{f:
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(f_0\|f)<\varepsilon
\right\}>0
\quad\text{for every }\varepsilon>0.
\tag{3}
$$

KL support ensures that the prior includes models with expected log likelihood
arbitrarily close to that of the truth.

# Support is important but not the whole theorem {#support-is-important-but-not-the-whole-theorem}

In infinite-dimensional problems, a prior may put positive mass near $f_0$ and
also place too much mass on enormous collections of highly irregular models
that track finite samples too closely. Standard consistency theorems therefore
combine ingredients such as

1. prior mass in KL neighborhoods of $f_0$;
2. tests that separate $f_0$ from alternatives;
3. sieve or entropy bounds controlling model complexity;
4. small prior mass outside well-behaved sieves.

At a nontechnical level:

- a **test** is a data-based rule that can distinguish $f_0$ from a separated
  collection of alternatives with errors that shrink as $n$ grows;
- a **sieve** is a sequence of manageable subsets of the large model space,
  allowed to grow with $n$;
- **entropy** here is a complexity count—roughly, how many small balls are
  needed to cover a model set—not Shannon entropy from information theory.

A “ball” of radius $\varepsilon$ around $f$ simply means a neighborhood
$\{g:d(f,g)<\varepsilon\}$ under the chosen metric.

These objects belong to proofs. You need to know why they appear, but not how
to construct them in order to read Walker's motivational chapter.

The exact conditions depend on the topology and the model. “The prior has full
support” is not a universal proof of posterior consistency.

# Reading Walker's display {#consistency-walker-display}

Walker writes the target in the form

$$
\Pi\{d(f,f_0)>\varepsilon\mid X_{1:n}\}
\longrightarrow0
\quad\text{a.s. }P_0^\infty.
$$

Read it in this order:

1. fix the true $f_0$ and radius $\varepsilon$;
2. identify the set of candidate densities outside that neighborhood;
3. compute the posterior probability of that set after $n$ observations;
4. view that posterior probability as a random variable because it depends on
   the random data;
5. ask whether that random variable converges to zero for almost every infinite
   sequence generated by $f_0$.

# Fractional or power posteriors {#consistency-fractional-posteriors}

For $0<\alpha\leq1$, a fractional posterior has

$$
\Pi_{n,\alpha}(df)
\propto L_n(f)^\alpha\Pi(df).
$$

Taking $\alpha<1$ reduces the data's weight relative to the prior. Walker
discusses a consistency argument in which a fractional likelihood can require
weaker support-related conditions than the ordinary $\alpha=1$ posterior
[@walker2001consistency; @walker2010bnp]. This is a specific theoretical result,
not a claim that every fractional posterior is automatically consistent.

# Consistency versus contraction rate

Consistency asks only whether posterior mass eventually enters every fixed
neighborhood. A stronger question asks how quickly the neighborhood may shrink:

$$
\Pi\{f:d(f,f_0)>M\varepsilon_n\mid X_{1:n}\}
\longrightarrow0,
$$

where $\varepsilon_n\downarrow0$. The sequence $\varepsilon_n$ is a posterior
contraction rate. Two priors can both be consistent yet learn at very different
rates.

The notation $\varepsilon_n\downarrow0$ means that the positive sequence
decreases toward zero. The radius $M\varepsilon_n$ is therefore allowed to
shrink with sample size, unlike the fixed $\varepsilon$ in ordinary
consistency.

# What consistency does not say

Posterior consistency does not by itself imply

- good finite-sample calibration;
- a fast contraction rate;
- correct uncertainty quantification for every functional;
- robustness to dependence when iid sampling was assumed;
- computational convergence of an MCMC algorithm.

It evaluates the learning rule, not every aspect of an analysis.

A **functional** is a numerical or finite-dimensional feature of the full
distribution, such as its mean, median, survival probability, or treatment
contrast. Learning the entire distribution in one metric does not
automatically calibrate every posterior credible interval for every such
feature.

# Check your understanding

Select each **Answer** box after working out the question yourself.

**1. With respect to which probability law is the almost-sure statement in (1)
made?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

It is made under $P_0^\infty$, the product probability law for the entire
infinite iid sequence generated from the fixed true distribution $P_0$. It is
not an almost-sure statement under the prior $\Pi$.
:::

**2. Why is the posterior probability in (1) itself random?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

For fixed $n$, the posterior probability is a function of the random data
$X_{1:n}$. A different sample generally produces a different posterior and
hence a different amount of mass outside the neighborhood of $f_0$.
:::

**3. What is the difference between weak and total-variation consistency?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

Weak consistency means the posterior concentrates in neighborhoods defined by
agreement of integrals of bounded continuous functions. Total-variation
consistency means concentration under

$$
d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)=\sup_A|P(A)-Q(A)|,
$$

which controls the largest discrepancy over all measurable events. Total
variation is therefore a stronger notion: convergence in total variation
implies weak convergence under the usual conditions, but not conversely.
:::

**4. Why can support alone be insufficient in an infinite-dimensional model?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

Positive prior mass near $f_0$ prevents the prior from ruling out the truth, but
the prior may also spread too much mass over vast collections of irregular
alternatives that fit finite samples well. Consistency proofs commonly also
need tests plus sieve, entropy, or tail-mass controls to keep that model
complexity manageable.
:::

**5. What extra information does a contraction rate provide?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

Ordinary consistency only says that posterior mass eventually enters every
fixed neighborhood. A contraction rate $\varepsilon_n\downarrow0$ describes
how quickly the posterior can concentrate inside a **shrinking** neighborhood,
for example one of radius $M\varepsilon_n$. It therefore permits comparison of
the learning speeds of two consistent priors.
:::
